prospects.name: Distinct Painters (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): Quote volume, 20 quotes/month, team of 8 painters.
Email 2 angle: Owner handles all quoting AND follow-up himself, that split alone is a bottleneck.
prospects.body:
Hi Distinct Painters,

Twenty quotes a month with a team of eight painters, you're the one writing the quotes, and you're the one following them up. That's a lot of time spent on the business of quoting rather than the craft of painting.

How do you decide which quotes to chase and which ones to let go?

Genuinely curious how owner-operators at your scale handle this.

Atlas

prospects.name: Adelaide Designer Painters (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): Designer/specialist positioning.
Email 2 angle: Different project types mean completely different quoting, a heritage restoration quote isn't the same as a new build.
prospects.body:
Hi Adelaide Designer Painters,

Designer and specialty work means you're not quoting the same job twice. Every project has its own scope, its own materials, its own timeline. Each quote is an investment of time before you've even won the work.

What's your process for staying on top of quotes that need follow-up weeks after they went out?

I ask because the businesses I talk to that do specialty work tend to feel this most acutely.

Atlas

prospects.name: Matte Projects Painting and Decorating (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): Project-based painting and decorating work.
Email 2 angle: Project-based work = sporadic quoting. Easy to lose track between jobs.
prospects.body:
Hi Matte Projects Painting and Decorating,

Project-based painting means your quoting isn't a steady drip, it comes in waves. A busy month might mean ten quotes out. A quiet month, two. The problem is the quiet month's quotes are the ones that matter most.

When work gets busy, what's the first thing that slips, quoting new work, or following up on quotes you've already sent?

Talking to a few painting businesses about how they handle this.

Atlas

prospects.name: All Melbourne Painting (Melbourne, VIC, contact: Kristian)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): Melbourne-wide coverage, city-scale operation.
Email 2 angle: City-wide coverage means more quotes, more moving parts, more to track.
prospects.body:
Hi All Melbourne Painting,

Covering a city the size of Melbourne, you're quoting jobs from Werribee to Ringwood. Different suburbs, different job types, different clients. Every quote is a bet on time you haven't been paid for yet.

Is there a point in the follow-up process where you usually stop hearing back, or does it vary job by job?

Just comparing notes across a few painting businesses.

Atlas

prospects.name: Performance Cleaning (Melbourne, VIC)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): Range of services, janitorial, office, commercial.
Email 2 angle: Process-focused. Two different business models in one company, recurring janitorial contracts vs one-off commercial quotes. Different quoting, different follow-up.
prospects.body:
Hi Performance Cleaning,

Janitorial contracts and one-off commercial jobs are two very different beasts. The recurring work has its own rhythm, but the one-off quotes, the office fitout clean, the end-of-lease job, those can slip through the cracks between regular service rounds.

How do you manage follow-up on commercial quotes when the day-to-day operations are running?

Curious how cleaning businesses balance this.

Atlas

prospects.name: Kleena Cleaners (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle (inferred): 38 years in the game, schools to industrial, guaranteed service.
Email 2 angle: Process-focused. Reputation built over decades, every quote that goes unanswered is a reflection on that guarantee.
prospects.body:
Hi Kleena Cleaners,

Thirty-eight years and a service guarantee carries a lot of weight. Every quote you send represents that reputation. When a quote goes out and you don't hear back, it's not just a lost job, it's a conversation that never finished.

Is follow-up on quotes something you track, or does it depend on the job and who's managing it?

Asking a few long-running businesses how they handle this.

Atlas

prospects.name: Click Click Media (Sydney, NSW)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle: Paid discovery model ($895/$2,895), Google Premier Partner 2026.
Email 2 angle: With a paid discovery model, you've already qualified the prospect before the proposal. The gap between proposal and decision must feel especially expensive.
prospects.body:
Hi Click Click Media,

Been thinking about the paid discovery model. Once a client's invested in the roadmap and you've delivered the strategic plan, the proposal that follows carries a lot more weight than a cold pitch. Which means every proposal you send after discovery is one you really can't afford to lose track of.

How do you manage the handover from strategy team to proposal delivery, and then the follow-up after that?

Curious how agencies with a paid-front-end model handle this end of the pipeline.

Atlas

prospects.name: Online Marketing Gurus (Sydney, NSW)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle: 200+ staff, GEO capabilities, 1,000+ clients.
Email 2 angle: Scale creates its own follow-up problem, with that many concurrent engagements, proposals that don't convert can get buried in the volume.
prospects.body:
Hi Online Marketing Gurus,

With 200-plus people and over a thousand Australian businesses in the portfolio, the volume of proposals going out must be significant. Not just new business proposals, existing clients getting proposals for additional services, GEO audits, expanded scope.

At that scale, is there a central view of what's out and what's still awaiting a decision, or does it live with the individual account managers?

Asking a few growth agencies how they handle this at different sizes.

Atlas

prospects.name: Next&Co (Melbourne, VIC)
prospects.subject: one more question
angles: Email 1 angle: Media buying, CRO, attribution, complex scoping work.
Email 2 angle: When scoping takes real work, the proposal itself represents significant invested time. The follow-up after that is just as important but often gets less attention.
prospects.body:
Hi Next&Co,

Media buying and CRO proposals aren't template work. Each one is scoped to the client's existing channels, performance data, and growth targets. That upfront investment means every proposal that goes quiet represents real time that can't be recovered.

I'm curious, after a proposal goes out, is there a structured follow-up cadence, or does it vary depending on who's managing the account?

Comparing notes across a few agencies on this.

Atlas
